The Aerosense measurement system uses low-cost, low-power MEMS sensors to measure local pressures, blade motions, and inflow conditions on wind turbine rotor blades.
The system is composed of sensor nodes installed on the blades, a base station that collects and transmits the data, and a digital twin system for data processing and analysis.
The sensor nodes measure the pressure distribution along the blade chord using 40 absolute pressure sensors, and the inflow conditions using 5 differential pressure sensors at the leading edge.

Thorough calibration and correction procedures are required to obtain accurate aerodynamic measurements on rotating blades, including corrections for atmospheric pressure, hydrostatic pressure, and centrifugal acceleration.
The researchers used a photogrammetry process to measure the 3D shape of the blade section and the precise positions of the pressure sensors.
On a 5MW wind turbine, the atmospheric pressure is about 50 times higher than the dynamic pressure, and the hydrostatic pressure variation is about 40% of the dynamic pressure.
After calibration, the root mean squared error between the reference pressure and the measured pressure was reduced from 87 Pa down to 11 Pa, a 1% precision for a multi-megawatt wind turbine.

The Aerosense system uses a hybrid method based on inviscid flow theory to infer the local angle of attack and wind speed from the differential pressure measurements, without requiring a reference pressure measurement.

Previous field measurement campaigns on wind turbine blades have faced challenges with the complex and costly installation of sensors inside the blades, issues with wiring sensors on a rotating system, and the need for extensive calibration and correction procedures.
The Aerosense system addresses the limitations of previous approaches by using a wireless and self-sufficient design that is easy to install, inexpensive, and non-intrusive to the blade.

The Aerosense measurements on the 7kW wind turbine showed that the pressure distribution can vary significantly during one rotation of the blade, even under stable wind conditions, due to misalignment of the wind direction with the turbine's rotational axis.
The Aerosense system is valuable for understanding the aerodynamic loading on rotor blades as well as the influence of the inflow conditions on wind turbine performance.

The Aerosense system includes a digital twin system that processes the field measurements, provides data analysis and visualization, and enables comparison and improvement of low and high-fidelity simulations.
The Aerosense system is designed to be a cost-effective solution for the wind energy industry, with easy installation, low cost, and non-intrusive hardware.
The Aerosense system can also be used to monitor the structural health of the blade, in addition to measuring the aerodynamic properties.
